title: The Giants Have Sails
boundary: Part I, chapter 8: first sight of the windmills through Sancho helping Quixote remount and their departure toward Puerto Lapice. Stop before the friars and Biscayan encounter. Context from I.7 is paraphrased: Sancho has joined as squire, hoping for a promised island.

sources.title: Two accounts of the same landscape
sources.quote: what we see there are not giants but windmills, and what seem to be their arms are the sails that turned by the wind make the millstone go.
sources.note: Sancho’s words offer a mechanism for what they see. The narrator has introduced thirty or forty windmills, while Quixote calls them giants. Perspective means a position or outlook that shapes interpretation; perspectives can differ without being equally supported.

sources.title: What happens at the mill
sources.quote: the wind whirled it round with such force that it shivered the lance to pieces, sweeping with it horse and rider, who went rolling over on the plain, in a sorry condition.
sources.note: Quixote charges despite Sancho’s warning. The narrator describes wind, sail, broken lance, and the fall. Students’ invented conversations do not prevent or replace this canonical event. Juxtaposition places things side by side; here heroic anticipation beside a mechanical collision exposes a gap.

sources.title: An explanation after the fall
sources.quote: that same sage Friston who carried off my study and books, has turned these giants into mills in order to rob me of the glory of vanquishing them
sources.note: Quixote claims an enchanter transformed the giants. He refers to an earlier explanation about his missing library; this episode does not reconstruct that intervening plot. The claim is his explanation, not an event the narrator confirms. Counterevidence is relevant evidence that challenges a claim or explanation.

scenes.title: Another line, another door
scenes.speaker: journal
text: Mr. Hepting sets an old journal on the desk. Its leather cover looks as if it has survived rain, travel, and a serious disagreement with a suitcase zipper.

‘I found this in an airport gift shop in Peru,’ he says. ‘Between the marmalade and the neck pillows. I asked it why boarding groups exist. I was gone three days.’ On the cover, someone has drawn a door. The little brass handle feels surprisingly real.

‘A new question on a new line,’ he says. ‘Then touch the door. It takes you somewhere you can investigate. Answers are your responsibility. So is coming back.’ I write a question. The page smells faintly of oranges. No classmates follow me: this small door is an invitation for one.

Today the page opens onto a road, not a courtyard. If this is my first visit, the journal supplies the essentials: Don Quixote has fashioned himself after knights from romances. Sancho Panza is his squire, a companion and assistant, hoping for a promised island to govern. I need no earlier episode or score to enter this page.

choices.label: How can I tell which account to trust?
choices.response: My question settles into the paper. A dry breeze turns the corner of the page. Somewhere beyond the door, somebody is using the word “giant” with alarming confidence.

choices.label: What happens when evidence challenges a story we love?
choices.response: I write my question and touch the drawn handle. The ink becomes a road. The journal has found an answerable problem; it has not promised an agreeable answer.

choices.label: How do I record a disagreement fairly?
choices.response: I write about fair records. Two lines run down the new page: “what happened” and “what people said.” For now they are empty. Keeping them separate already feels useful.

scenes.title: A chronicler on the plain
scenes.speaker: sancho
text: I step onto a dusty road in La Mancha. Sancho Panza turns on his donkey and introduces himself. Ahead, Don Quixote sits upright on Rocinante as if posture alone could put the whole countryside in order.

Quixote appoints me chronicler for the journey: a witness who will put the day into words. ‘I hope you brought enough paper,’ Sancho says. ‘His adventures can become larger in the telling.’ My task is to record a disagreement without pretending I can command either man.

White towers stand across the plain, with long wooden sails. Quixote announces giants. Sancho says windmills. The journal lays the two accounts side by side. I can already see a problem: a description can fit an expectation so neatly that the expectation starts looking like evidence.

choices.label: I ask Sancho why he came on this journey.
choices.response: He mentions the island he hopes to govern, then pats his food bag. ‘A man can want an island and still recognize a mill.’ Practical observation and aspiration can live in one person. I resist making him a simple opposite of Quixote.

choices.label: I ask what Quixote sees.
choices.response: ‘An opportunity to serve,’ he says. ‘And arms of unusual length.’ His wish to do something meaningful is clear. Whether those shapes are arms is a separate question. My sympathy does not make the shapes into bodies.

margin.text: Cervantes leans around the page’s lower corner. “Two witnesses are useful. Two witness statements are not automatically two equally good explanations. What would let you compare them?”

followups.a: “It changes what someone notices and how someone interprets it. Then ask what the text actually reports. Fairness to a voice need not mean surrendering your judgment of its evidence.”

scenes.title: Arms, sails, and a working explanation
scenes.speaker: sancho
text: Sancho points to the sails. He describes wind turning them so that a millstone can grind grain. His explanation connects the visible motion to the object’s function. Quixote describes long arms and prepares for battle.

The source does not leave us with an undecidable landscape: the narrator calls the objects windmills. Still, I need to do more than say Sancho is the sensible character. An evidence entry should specify what supports his account, and avoid inventing observations I have not made.
The sails begin to move. My notebook wants a distinction between observation and interpretation before the road becomes considerably less peaceful.

choices.label: The narrator identifies windmills; Sancho explains their wind-driven sails. Quixote interprets those sails as arms.
choices.response: I preserve the difference between the described object and the knight’s interpretation. The explanation of a mechanism is relevant support, not just a confident label.

choices.label: I cite the narrator’s windmills and Sancho’s account, then record Quixote’s giant claim as a conflicting interpretation.
choices.response: Both statements remain visible. Their evidential standing does not become equal merely because both are recorded. I identify who says each thing and what supports it.

choices.label: Because two people disagree, giants and windmills must be equally likely.
choices.response: Disagreement alone does not balance the evidence. I return to the narrator’s description and Sancho’s mechanism, rather than counting opinions.

scenes.title: A warning that might not work
scenes.speaker: quixote
text: Quixote adjusts his lance. I have one chance to speak before he moves. My appointment gives me a voice, not authority over his decisions.

A specific observation could challenge him directly. A question could invite him to test his own account. Either can be sound; either can fail to persuade. Mockery might make me feel certain while making him less willing to listen. The learning credit is in my evidence entries, not whether he approves of my intervention.
I stay beside Sancho, clear of the moving sails. Which approach will I try?

choices.label: I point to the wind-driven sails and ask him to pause before charging.
choices.response: ‘You see machinery where I see injustice,’ he says. My warning is specific and unsuccessful. Sancho calls after him too. Neither of us gets to control what he does next.

choices.label: I ask what observation would persuade him that these are mills.
choices.response: For a moment he looks back. ‘A useful question after the victory.’ He postpones the test and spurs Rocinante. The question opens a crack in the conversation, then confidence closes it.

choices.label: I laugh at him and tell him nobody sensible sees giants.
choices.response: His shoulders stiffen. ‘Then courage has become unfashionable.’ I have challenged his identity without showing the evidence. Sancho still warns him about the mills. My laughter has not protected anyone.

scenes.title: The world answers in wood
scenes.speaker: quixote
text: Rocinante carries him toward the first mill. A breeze turns the sails. Quixote charges; his lance strikes a sail, breaks, and horse and rider tumble onto the plain. I remain safely with Sancho. No choice of mine rewrites this event.

For an instant there is no grand speech. There is a broken lance and a man who needs help. Sancho goes to him and helps him rise. I hold my journal shut against the dust. The comedy has not removed the pain.

Juxtaposition puts things beside each other so that their relationship becomes noticeable. Irony involves a gap between a claim or expectation and what the text lets us understand. Here heroic anticipation meets the ordinary workings of a mill. What does that arrangement do?

choices.label: The heroic expectation is set beside a mechanical collision; the gap makes the confidence ironic and the harm visible.
choices.response: I explain how the juxtaposition creates an ironic gap, while keeping the physical consequences in view. The scene can be funny and troubling at the same time.

choices.label: The narrator and Sancho identify mills before the charge, so the reader anticipates a collision that Quixote interprets as combat.
choices.response: I connect the order of information to the reader’s understanding. The irony comes from what we know beside what he believes; “something funny happens” would not explain the form.

choices.label: Irony simply means that Quixote is stupid and Sancho is always right.
choices.response: That replaces an explanation of the text with two labels. I should identify the claim, the evidence, and the gap in this scene. Nothing here proves that Sancho is infallible in every situation.

margin.text: Cervantes sets his quill down. “You may laugh before the fall. Now a hand reaches toward him. What does that change about the kind of laughter this scene allows?”

followups.a: “Try holding the broken lance and the wish to help in the same account. Sympathy can ask why a belief matters; criticism can ask whether it fits the evidence. Neither needs to erase the other.”

scenes.title: The explanation that survives everything
scenes.speaker: quixote
text: Quixote says the enchanter Friston has turned the giants into mills to rob him of glory. He refers to an earlier account of his vanished library. The narrator reports his explanation without confirming that a transformation happened.

Sancho’s mouth tightens. He has already identified windmills before the charge. The knight can make that inconvenient detail disappear by adding more magic, but I need to ask what could then count against the explanation.

Counterevidence is relevant evidence that challenges a claim. If every possible result becomes proof of the same claim, an explanation stops being open to correction. My journal will not write “false because I dislike it.” It asks for a reason.

choices.label: Sancho identifies mills before the charge; a transformation after defeat does not account for that earlier observation.
choices.response: The timing matters. I identify counterevidence rather than relying on ridicule. Quixote could add an earlier enchantment, but that would be a new claim needing support.

choices.label: The narrator supplies mills and mechanical causes, while the transformation lacks confirmation; I ask what evidence could challenge it.
choices.response: I weigh support and name a test of openness to revision. I cannot prove every imaginable magic impossible; I can show why this explanation is less supported by this passage.

choices.label: Because magic explains any outcome, the transformation must be true.
choices.response: An explanation’s flexibility is not evidence that it happened. I need support for the transformation and attention to the mills identified before the charge.

scenes.title: From a road to an argument
scenes.speaker: sancho
text: Sancho helps Quixote remount. He does not withdraw his description of the mills. Being right has not made his companion unhurt, and assistance does not require him to adopt the giant story.

I think about a claim outside this journey: a rumor, a heroic narrative, an advertisement, or my own first interpretation of a text. When a result goes badly, it is tempting to protect the original story with an explanation that nothing could challenge.
A useful connection will transfer a method, not declare that modern people and a Spanish literary character are identical. What should I carry back from this disagreement?

choices.label: For another claim, separate observations from explanations and ask what would count against it; then check relevant evidence.
choices.response: The method transfers while the contexts remain different. I could use it on an advertisement or another literary interpretation without treating either as the same story.

choices.label: Compare this with a specific hero’s response to a setback: what evidence is available, and does the hero revise or protect the original belief?
choices.response: The question invites a passage-based comparison. It does not assume that every hero responds in the same way. I leave a space for the other text and its different circumstances.

choices.label: Anyone with a hopeful dream is just another Don Quixote, so dreams should be abandoned.
choices.response: The analogy erases the difference between aspiration and disregard for evidence. This encounter challenges a particular belief and its defense, not every possible hope.

margin.text: Cervantes lets a few grains of dust fall off the margin. “A comparison is a bridge, not a machine for making everything identical. Which difference would your bridge need to leave visible?”

followups.a: “There can be several defensible accounts of hope, self-invention, and resistance to evidence. Show which details support yours and what it leaves unexplained. My approving expression is not a quotation from the novel.”

scenes.title: What the witness leaves on the page
scenes.speaker: quixote
text: The road continues toward Puerto Lapice. Quixote still expects adventures. Sancho still has practical concerns. The sails turn behind us, grinding grain with no apparent interest in reputation.

I cannot claim that my argument changed the knight. I can decide how to record a conversation that failed. The account must make his hope intelligible without giving his explanation evidence it does not have.

My journal reopens to the question that brought me here. I may write what I discovered and what remains uncertain. I have witnessed a canonical event; I have also learned that a strong reason and a successful persuasion are different things.

choices.label: I record the mills and fall as events, and his enchantment story as a claim, adding why the earlier evidence challenges it.
choices.response: Quixote dislikes the word “claim.” I leave it there, with his reasons beside it. Sancho asks me to include that he helped. I do: his assistance shows care without surrendering judgment.

choices.label: I preserve both voices, then explain why the narrator’s details and Sancho’s mechanism support the mill account.
choices.response: Neither voice disappears. I make the difference in evidential support clear. Quixote requests a more heroic title. I can offer a respectful title without changing the facts underneath it.

choices.label: I call the defeated giants a victory and omit the mill evidence.
choices.response: He approves. My evidence notebook does not. The journal keeps my chosen account beside the details I recorded, so I can see where I protected approval at the expense of an explanation. The episode ends with that revision still available to me.

options: Sancho sounds confident, so no evidence is needed.
The narrator identifies mills; Sancho explains the wind-driven sails.
Two accounts must be equally supported.
driverQuestions.note: Compare specific evidence and mechanisms, not confidence or the number of opinions.

driverQuestions.prompt: What produces irony in the charge?
options: The reader knows the objects are mills while Quixote acts as if they are giants.
The narrator confirms a real transformation.
driverQuestions.note: The gap between the reader’s supported understanding and the knight’s belief shapes the scene.

driverQuestions.prompt: Which detail challenges a transformation after the defeat?
options: Sancho identifies windmills before the charge.
driverQuestions.note: Earlier mill identification is counterevidence to an explanation that places transformation after defeat.

driverQuestions.prompt: What can a fair account do?
options: Remove Quixote’s voice because he is wrong.
Preserve both voices and explain why their claims have different support.
Treat sympathy as proof of giants.
driverQuestions.note: Fair representation and evidence-based judgment can coexist; failed persuasion does not invalidate strong reasoning.
